posts.title: Liability Management Ate Operational Restructuring
posts.excerpt: The balance sheet gets fixed in six weeks and the business gets fixed never. That trade is why the same names keep coming back.
posts.plain: There used to be a sequence. A company ran out of room, someone did the work of figuring out why, and the capital structure got rebuilt around whatever the business could actually support, the financial fix downstream of the operating diagnosis, not a substitute for it. That sequence is mostly gone. The financial fix happens first now. Fast. Often instead. That range is the whole story in one statistic: the dominant resolution mechanism in credit is now a transaction reasonable people disagree about whether to even call a default. Sources: Moody's, US corporate default risk in 2026; Moody's via Business Standard on repeat defaulters.
posts.body:
There used to be a sequence. A company ran out of room, someone did the work of figuring out why, and the capital structure got rebuilt around whatever the business could actually support, the financial fix downstream of the operating diagnosis, not a substitute for it.

That sequence is mostly gone. The financial fix happens first now. Fast. Often instead.

## The numbers say the exchange is the default

Moody's put roughly 65% of private credit defaults in 2025 in the distressed restructuring bucket, not chapter 11, exchanges. The measured default rate for private credit last year sits anywhere between 1.6% and 4.7%, depending entirely on whether you count those exchanges as defaults at all. That range is the whole story in one statistic: the dominant resolution mechanism in credit is now a transaction reasonable people disagree about whether to even call a default.

## What an LME actually buys

Maturity runway. A lower cash coupon. That's it. Both real, both valuable; neither, however, is an answer to why the business stopped generating cash in the first place.

An operational restructuring is slow and unpleasant: you close locations, exit product lines, fight with management about a cost base they built and still believe in. It takes quarters, and it makes enemies. An uptier takes six weeks, needs a majority rather than consensus, and pays fees to the people who execute it. Given those two options, and a sponsor whose equity is already out of the money, the choice makes itself. Nobody in the room is incentivized to run the slow one.

## The bill arrives as recidivism

Moody's counted repeat offenders as roughly 40% of US corporate defaults in 2023. That number is the price of treating a leverage problem as a maturity problem. The mechanism isn't complicated: a company can't service debt because the business is impaired; an LME cuts cash interest and pushes maturities out two or three years; nothing changes operationally, because nothing in the deal required it to. Two or three years later, less liquidity, worse docs, fewer unencumbered assets, and a lender group that's already been through one fight.

Round two is always worse than round one. The easy collateral is pledged. The unrestricted-subsidiary capacity is used. The cooperative lenders have already been sorted from the excluded ones.

## What I'd actually watch

Not the LME announcement. The twelve months after it.

If the exchange comes with a genuine operating plan, new management, a closed footprint, a cost program with dates attached, treat it as a bridge. If it comes with a press release about "enhanced financial flexibility" and no change to how the company is actually run, price it as a delay and start diligencing the next capital structure now.

The second one is more common. The balance sheet gets fixed in six weeks. The business gets fixed never. And the market keeps paying full price for it anyway.

---

*Sources: Moody's, [US corporate default risk in 2026](https://www.moodys.com/web/en/us/insights/credit-risk/private-credit/us-corporate-default-risk-in-2026.html); Moody's via [Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/amp/world-news/repeat-offenders-made-up-40-of-us-corporate-defaults-in-2023-moody-s-124041601273_1.html) on repeat defaulters.*

posts.title: The 2027 Wall Isn't Big. It's Badly Sorted.
posts.excerpt: Over $700bn of high yield comes due 2027–2029. The size is manageable. What isn't manageable is who's left standing in front of it.
posts.plain: Everyone calls it a wall. Which is the wrong word, because it puts the emphasis on height, and height was never the issue here. The size, first Start with the numbers, because they're the part people get wrong. More than $700 billion of US high yield matures across 2027–2029, over $350 billion of that landing in 2029 alone, and if you throw in leveraged loans and speculative grade maturities, 2028 by itself runs to something like $1 trillion. Those are big figures and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But 2025 high yield issuance cleared $325 billion, up 17%, the strongest year since 2021 — and on pure volume, the market absorbs this without blinking. Three years of ordinary issuance against three years of maturities. If this were only a capacity question, we'd be done here. It's not a capacity question. The composition is the whole problem Two numbers from 2025, sitting next to each other, that should make you uneasy. Over 70% of issuance was refinancing, the highest share since 2009. Straight CCC paper: under 2% of issuance, second lowest on record. Put those next to each other and the story writes itself. The market spent all of 2025 refinancing everything that could be refinanced, and touched almost nothing rated CCC while doing it. Which means what's sitting in front of 2027 and 2028 isn't a random sample of the credit universe. It's what's left over, the names that tried to term out into a wide open market and couldn't. Why that matters more than the total A wall of BB paper is a calendar problem. A wall built from three years of "everyone who could refinance already did" is something else entirely, a default pipeline wearing a scheduling problem's name. The issuers still standing in front of 2027 are there for a reason, usually one of two: they tried and the market said no, or they saw the clearing spread and decided to wait it out. Waiting doesn't fix either problem. What actually breaks first Not the maturity date on the calendar. Long before that: springing covenants, cash sweeps that trigger 12 to 18 months out, and, quietly, in parallel, an auditor asking uncomfortable going concern questions. That's where the real clock starts, which means the actual distress shows up through late 2026 and 2027, not on the day a bond technically comes due. By the time you're looking at a maturity date, the outcome already got decided, a year earlier, in a room you weren't in. The practical read Forget the aggregate. Track three things instead: the ratings distribution of what's still outstanding by maturity year, how many refi attempts get launched and then pulled before pricing, and how much extension activity shows up, because that's the tell that a full refinancing wasn't actually on the table. The size was never the story. Who's left in front of it is. Sources: PitchBook, 2026 US High Yield Outlook; Octus, 2026 Distressed Outlook.
posts.body:
Everyone calls it a wall. Which is the wrong word, because it puts the emphasis on height, and height was never the issue here.

## The size, first

Start with the numbers, because they're the part people get wrong. More than $700 billion of US high yield matures across 2027–2029, over $350 billion of that landing in 2029 alone, and if you throw in leveraged loans and speculative-grade maturities, 2028 by itself runs to something like $1 trillion. Those are big figures and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But 2025 high yield issuance cleared $325 billion, up 17%, the strongest year since 2021 — and on pure volume, the market absorbs this without blinking. Three years of ordinary issuance against three years of maturities. If this were only a capacity question, we'd be done here.

It's not a capacity question.

## The composition is the whole problem

Two numbers from 2025, sitting next to each other, that should make you uneasy. Over 70% of issuance was refinancing, the highest share since 2009. Straight CCC paper: under 2% of issuance, second-lowest on record. Put those next to each other and the story writes itself. The market spent all of 2025 refinancing everything that could be refinanced, and touched almost nothing rated CCC while doing it. Which means what's sitting in front of 2027 and 2028 isn't a random sample of the credit universe. It's what's left over, the names that tried to term out into a wide-open market and couldn't.

## Why that matters more than the total

A wall of BB paper is a calendar problem. A wall built from three years of "everyone who could refinance already did" is something else entirely, a default pipeline wearing a scheduling problem's name. The issuers still standing in front of 2027 are there for a reason, usually one of two: they tried and the market said no, or they saw the clearing spread and decided to wait it out. Waiting doesn't fix either problem.

## What actually breaks first

Not the maturity date on the calendar. Long before that: springing covenants, cash sweeps that trigger 12 to 18 months out, and, quietly, in parallel, an auditor asking uncomfortable going-concern questions. That's where the real clock starts, which means the actual distress shows up through late 2026 and 2027, not on the day a bond technically comes due. By the time you're looking at a maturity date, the outcome already got decided, a year earlier, in a room you weren't in.

## The practical read

Forget the aggregate. Track three things instead: the ratings distribution of what's still outstanding by maturity year, how many refi attempts get launched and then pulled before pricing, and how much extension activity shows up, because that's the tell that a full refinancing wasn't actually on the table.

The size was never the story. Who's left in front of it is.

---

*Sources: [PitchBook, 2026 US High-Yield Outlook](https://pitchbook.com/news/articles/2026-us-high-yield-outlook-volume-to-tick-higher-amid-looming-maturity-wall); [Octus, 2026 Distressed Outlook](https://octus.com/resources/articles/2026-distressed-outlook/).*

posts.title: Serta Gets a Number: $261m, Plus Six Years of Interest
posts.excerpt: Judge Lopez put a price on an improper uptier. The damages math is more instructive than the liability finding, and it lands almost entirely on prejudgment interest.
posts.plain: A number, finally. On July 7, 2026, Judge Christopher Lopez in the Southern District of Texas entered judgment against the participating lenders in Serta: roughly $400 million, of which $261.13 million is the judgment itself and the rest — nearly a third of the total — is New York statutory prejudgment interest, running at 9% since June 22, 2020. Sit with that split. A third of the exposure isn't the deal. It's the clock. The liability half is now settled law in the Fifth Circuit The 2020 exchange was not an "open market purchase," however the participating lenders wanted to characterize it. The court treated it as a payment in respect of principal, which triggered the pro rata sharing provision, which those lenders did not satisfy. This is the reading the excluded lenders have been pressing since 2020, and it has now survived, in full, through to a damages award. The argument that an open market purchase exception can cover a negotiated, non ratable exchange among a hand picked majority is finished, at least in this circuit. The damages half is where the actual lesson sits The court rejected the models built off Serta's 2023 chapter 11 emergence and instead valued the breach as of the breach date, marking the first lien loans at 25 cents. That choice does two things at once. It caps the claim at what the position was worth in June 2020, rather than letting excluded lenders capture the full downstream consequences of the transaction, a real limit, and a meaningful one for anyone modeling recovery. But it also front loads the clock: a 2020 breach date means six years of 9% statutory interest accrue before anyone gets paid, and that second effect swamps the first. New York prejudgment interest is not discretionary, it is not compounded at some negotiated market rate, and it accrues whether the litigation moves quickly or not. Six years of it turns a $261 million judgment into a $400 million one. Two structural details worth carrying forward There's no joint liability here. Each defendant answers only for its proportional share of first lien holdings as of June 22, 2020 — a participating lender's exposure is a function of its own ticket, not the group's. That changes the settlement dynamics entirely: no single deep pocket to chase, no contribution fight among defendants. And breach date valuation cuts both ways. Excluded lenders who assumed damages would be measured against a reorganized enterprise got substantially less than they modeled. If you're underwriting uptier litigation as a recovery strategy, run breach date marks. Not emergence date ones. Where it goes Expect the Fifth Circuit again. But the practical effect is already priced into how deals get done: the open market purchase exception is now a drafted, fought over provision instead of boilerplate, and getting it wrong finally has a public number attached. That number is the useful part. Not the precedent. The invoice. Sources: Vinson & Elkins on the Serta damages judgment; Octus on the damages math and the rejected mitigation defense.
posts.body:
A number, finally. On July 7, 2026, Judge Christopher Lopez in the Southern District of Texas entered judgment against the participating lenders in Serta: roughly $400 million, of which $261.13 million is the judgment itself and the rest — nearly a third of the total — is New York statutory prejudgment interest, running at 9% since June 22, 2020.

Sit with that split. A third of the exposure isn't the deal. It's the clock.

## The liability half is now settled law in the Fifth Circuit

The 2020 exchange was not an "open market purchase," however the participating lenders wanted to characterize it. The court treated it as a payment in respect of principal, which triggered the pro rata sharing provision, which those lenders did not satisfy. This is the reading the excluded lenders have been pressing since 2020, and it has now survived, in full, through to a damages award. The argument that an open-market-purchase exception can cover a negotiated, non-ratable exchange among a hand-picked majority is finished, at least in this circuit.

## The damages half is where the actual lesson sits

The court rejected the models built off Serta's 2023 chapter 11 emergence and instead valued the breach as of the breach date, marking the first lien loans at 25 cents. That choice does two things at once. It caps the claim at what the position was worth in June 2020, rather than letting excluded lenders capture the full downstream consequences of the transaction, a real limit, and a meaningful one for anyone modeling recovery. But it also front-loads the clock: a 2020 breach date means six years of 9% statutory interest accrue before anyone gets paid, and that second effect swamps the first.

New York prejudgment interest is not discretionary, it is not compounded at some negotiated market rate, and it accrues whether the litigation moves quickly or not. Six years of it turns a $261 million judgment into a $400 million one.

## Two structural details worth carrying forward

There's no joint liability here. Each defendant answers only for its proportional share of first lien holdings as of June 22, 2020 — a participating lender's exposure is a function of its own ticket, not the group's. That changes the settlement dynamics entirely: no single deep pocket to chase, no contribution fight among defendants.

And breach-date valuation cuts both ways. Excluded lenders who assumed damages would be measured against a reorganized enterprise got substantially less than they modeled. If you're underwriting uptier litigation as a recovery strategy, run breach-date marks. Not emergence-date ones.

## Where it goes

Expect the Fifth Circuit again. But the practical effect is already priced into how deals get done: the open-market-purchase exception is now a drafted, fought-over provision instead of boilerplate, and getting it wrong finally has a public number attached.

That number is the useful part. Not the precedent. The invoice.

---

*Sources: [Vinson & Elkins on the Serta damages judgment](https://www.velaw.com/insights/serta-bankruptcy-court-awards-approximately-400-million-judgment-following-fifth-circuit-uptier-ruling/); [Octus on the damages math and the rejected mitigation defense](https://octus.com/resources/articles/expert-views-the-cost-of-an-improper-uptier-inside-sertas-damages/).*

posts.title: Why This Exists
posts.excerpt: A running notebook on restructuring — dockets, docs, and the arguments that keep repeating.
posts.plain: This is a notebook, not a newsletter. I read a lot of dockets and credit agreements and I want somewhere to put the patterns down before I forget them. Expect posts on chapter 11 mechanics, liability management, creditor coalitions, and the occasional rant about disclosure statements. Nothing here is investment or legal advice.
